hypotheses.basis: The word 'necessary' indicates only-if direction: cancellation requires ownership and confirmation as prerequisites, but does not guarantee sufficiency. 'For a pending order' is treated as an additional necessary condition within the same scope. Violations occur when cancel_order happens while any required condition is absent.
unresolved_terms: sufficiency of the listed conditions
whether other unstated conditions may also be necessary

hypotheses.basis: 'For a pending order' is read as a scope qualifier limiting the policy's applicability rather than a checkable condition. Within that scope, ownership and confirmation are necessary. Non-pending orders fall outside the policy entirely, so their cancellation is neither permitted nor prohibited by this rule.
unresolved_terms: policy treatment of non-pending order cancellations
whether scope qualifier or condition is intended

hypotheses.basis: The phrase 'necessary before cancellation' for pending orders could impose a positive obligation to ensure ownership and confirmation are established whenever an order is in pending state, independent of whether cancellation is attempted. The violation is the state-of-affairs deficiency (pending order lacking required conditions) rather than the action of canceling without them.
unresolved_terms: whether the obligation is discharged by the mere presence of conditions or requires active verification
who bears the obligation (system vs. requester)

hypotheses.basis: The policy scopes its constraint to 'a pending order,' which could be read as implicitly permitting cancellation of non-pending orders without any ownership or confirmation requirement. Unlike the existing scope-qualifier reading that leaves non-pending cancellations unaddressed, this reading actively permits them, changing the default from 'no rule applies' to 'cancellation is allowed.'
unresolved_terms: whether 'for a pending order' is an exclusive scope limiter (only pending orders are constrained) or an inclusive one (pending orders are at least constrained, others may have other rules)
